A.explanation: The ratio $(1 \times 10^{-3})/(2 \times 10^{-6}) = 500$, so the second current is 500 times larger.

B.explanation: This is 10 times too large, from an error in the factor of 2 or in counting powers of 10 between micro and milli.

C.explanation: This confuses the prefixes, for example treating $1 \text{ mA}$ as $1 \text{ A}$ when dividing by $2 \text{ } \mu\text{A}$.

D.explanation: This is far too large and comes from misplacing powers of 10 when converting milli and micro to ampere.

hints: Notice the two readings use different SI prefixes: $2 \text{ } \mu\text{A}$ in the first circuit and $1 \text{ mA}$ in the second circuit.
Recall that micro means $10^{-6}$ and milli means $10^{-3}$, so convert both currents to ampere before comparing.
Form the ratio second current divided by first current: $(1 \times 10^{-3} \text{ A})/(2 \times 10^{-6} \text{ A})$ and simplify the powers of 10.
walkthrough: Identify the given currents: first circuit $I_1 = 2 \text{ } \mu\text{A}$ and second circuit $I_2 = 1 \text{ mA}$.
Use SI prefix values: $1 \text{ } \mu\text{A} = 10^{-6} \text{ A}$ and $1 \text{ mA} = 10^{-3} \text{ A}$.
Convert to ampere: $I_1 = 2 \times 10^{-6} \text{ A}$ and $I_2 = 1 \times 10^{-3} \text{ A}$.
Set up the comparison as a ratio: $I_2/I_1 = (1 \times 10^{-3})/(2 \times 10^{-6})$.
Calculate: $(1/2) \times 10^{(-3 - (-6))} = 0.5 \times 10^3 = 500$ with no unit, as expected for a ratio.
A factor of 500 matches the listed value 500. This is option A.
